title: Diversify probe signals and SLO-driven admission controller for regional autoscale stability
creator: Ethan Zhao
description:
Problem: We observe periodic autoscaler instability during mixed workloads (long chat sessions + short completions) across regions. Liveness/readiness probes are overly homogeneous (single HTTP healthz and synthetic short-completion check), causing correlated probe failures and noisy scale decisions; regional failovers amplify oscillation and trigger circuit breakers too aggressively. SLOs (p99 latency and error budget burn) are at risk when autoscaling overshoots or sheds capacity too late.

Goal: Reduce correlated probe noise, enforce SLO-aware admission decisions earlier, and make autoscaling more stable across regions and workload mixes. Deliverables: (1) probe diversification (passive + targeted synthetic + KV-cache warmness checks), (2) an SLO-driven admission controller that applies token-aware request shaping and soft circuit-breaker signals to upstream routers, (3) a sliding-window SLO-enforcement policy used by autoscaler to prefer steady-state capacity over reactive ramping, and (4) simulation harness + dashboard to validate behavior before rollout.

Proposal summary:
- Probe diversification: add three orthogonal signals per instance: (A) passive latency window (quantiles from the last 30s of actual requests), (B) synthetic warmup probes that exercise long-sequence KV cache & batching (low-frequency, ramping from 1/min to 1/s per instance during canary), (C) dependency probes (eg. GPU driver/disks/KV store) that are lightweight but catch resource degradation early. Readiness becomes an AND of (A OR B) with C as a gating signal for severe infra issues instead of immediate eviction.
- Sliding-window SLO enforcement: compute burn-rate and latency violations on a 5m rolling window and expose an "autoscale bias" metric [-1.0, +1.0] that nudges scale decisions toward conservatism when transient spikes are detected. The autoscaler will use this bias to prefer smaller step changes and longer cool-downs when bias < -0.2 (indicating recent SLO risk).
- Admission controller & soft circuit breaker: implement an admission policy at the edge router that (i) classifies requests by expected cost (short vs long vs streaming), (ii) applies per-token concurrency caps and priority tiers, and (iii) emits soft circuit-breaker signals (warning states) to autoscaler and regional router so degraded capacity can be steered rather than fully rejected. Token-aware shedding reduces tail impact on short requests while allowing long-running sessions to finish with degraded throughput.
- Multi-region failover coordination: add cross-region health-weight smoothing so when a region degrades, traffic is stepped down gradually to avoid sudden worldwide influx; maintain per-region failover limits controlled by policy (eg. max 15%/minute shift).

Implementation notes: Start with a feature flag (ff:probe_diversify_slo_admission) to enable behavior per deployment. Probe agents will run in the same pod process to avoid network flakiness biasing signals. The admission controller will be implemented in the router (Go) and expose metrics via Prometheus with dedicated labels (request_class, token_estimate, admission_action).

Testing & verification:
- Simulation harness: extend ENG-68211's probe sim (see design doc) to generate mixed workloads and validate autoscaler bias effects. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1205 (WIP).
- Canary plan: enable for 5% traffic in east-us, monitor p99 latency, error budget, autoscale oscillation metric for 72h, then expand to 25%/72h and regionally to eu-west.
- Dashboards: new dashboard runtime/slo/admission with burn-rate, autoscale-bias, probe-signal-fusion, admission-drop-rate per region. Draft: https://dashboards.redwood.local/d/runtime/slo-admission (internal).

Trade-offs and open questions:
- Increasing synthetic probes increases load and could bias batching behavior; we'll keep synthetic frequency conservative and tie activation to canary windows.
- Admission controller complexity: token-estimate models must be calibrated; initial implementation will use heuristic token cost buckets derived from current payload stats.
- Backward compatibility: ensure older console components that rely on simple liveness don't break by keeping previous endpoints until rollout completes.

Rollout steps:
1) Merge probe and metric changes behind flag (runtime-1.22 branch).
2) Lab validation + sim runs (2 days).
3) Small canary in one AZ (5% traffic) for 72h.
4) Regional canary (25%) 72h.
5) Global staged rollout with monitoring gates.

Success criteria:
- 30% reduction in autoscaler step-change frequency during mixed workloads in sim.
- No increase in p99 latency > 5% in canary regions.
- Lowerized circuit-breaker hard trips (>=50% reduction) during degraded infra events in test scenarios.
